title: I spent 3 years reverse engineering and rebuilding a dead MMO. AI can now do it in a day.
author: renewal_re
selftext:
There was a 2D isometric MMO that I played when I was young. In 2004, the servers shut down, and because there were no private servers or captured server packets, no one has been able to play it since.

In 2023, I finally decided to resurrect the game.

I combed through the original CD. All of the assets and data were stored in a custom binary format. There was no documentation for it, so I spent dozens of hours decoding sprites, visual effects, animations, maps, and items, simply by looking at raw hex and figuring it out.

I cataloged every asset. I rebuilt the map loader, the UI, the sprite handler, the login and character system, and the combat controller.

The code became completely unmaintainable, so I rebuilt an ECS game engine from scratch. I built my own networking layer optimized for real-time online games. I implemented replay, rollback, and client prediction.

"You can't build an MMO solo," everyone said.

Well, I was going to try. And I was really sure I would succeed.

I've sunk well over **1,000 hours** into this.

Sure, AI can vibecode an entire SaaS, but there's no way it could reverse engineer an old Windows game and rebuild an entire massive multiplayer online game, right?

---

When I started in 2023, the game had been dead for 20+ years, and I was the only one attempting to resurrect it.

Yet in October 2026 alone, **3 other engineers started working on reverse engineering the same game.**

It now takes AI less than 20 minutes to study the original client files, reconstruct the entire world, and get a character walking around the map.

I tried it myself over the weekend.

In that time, I was able to implement:

- Multiplayer
- Combat and spells
- Mob spawning and combat AI
- Experience, stats, and leveling
- NPCs and merchants
- Banking

It was also able to:

- Port the entire game to modern macOS.
- Reverse engineer the network protocols and emulate the server-side protocol within minutes.
- Add WASD controls to a 20-year-old game.
- Increase the resolution beyond 640x480 by rendering more tiles.

I didn't have to provide any technical direction. I simply told it what feature I wanted and left it alone for 15 minutes.

---

I'm really not sure what to do now.

I spent 10+ years accumulating experience in frontend, backend, mobile, devops, security, architecture, cloud, and UX.

I moved away from full-stack development because it looked like AI was coming for it. I moved into real-time multiplayer, believing that it would be safe because it required combining all of my expertise.

But apparently AI can do that too, at a speed 100x faster than me.

---

I used to pride myself on my ability to cut scope and ship a working product. Many people can write code, but few people actually finish and deliver.

Well, it turns out everyone can ship now. The other 3 engineers already have a server running.

**Who needs to cut scope when AI can code things as fast as you can think of them?**

I always wrote clean, maintainable code that's easy to understand and easy to change without introducing bugs.

**Who needs good software practices when AI can apparently navigate a 20-year-old .exe and extend it just fine?**

For the first time in over 10 years, I'm genuinely worried about my job and my future.

comments.author: krazyjakee
comments.body: I'd focus on your product skills instead of your technical ones. At this time, AI struggles with game feel, taste and creativity. It's context limit prevents the folding together of the thousands of "little things" that make an experience come together. There's a great book called "Tynan Sylvester's Designing Games: A Guide to Engineering Experiences" from the creator of rimworld. It spells out very, very human centric game design. AI has solved engineering but great, cohesive experiences still require humans.

It used to be that you had to know how to code and have persistence to ship. Now there is no need to know how to code - just persistence, and much less of it than before. 

  
Sure, most of vibe coded projects now are unfinished slop, only because we have Opus 5.5 level models for a month or so. Imagine what will be there in a year.

  
Sure, probably 95% of those Photoshop clones will die. But you know what? 5% will go on. 

  
There is a SolidCraft alpha/beta released now. Easy to use open source mechanical CAD. We NEVER had this before because there were not enough people with skill, will and persistence to make it. Now it is already usable for basic stuff.

And then I started stress testing it, at first having 10 player on one map killing mobs was a problem. Now i'm still aiming for 50 players and it's still an issue (on a 2 vCPU VPS not my 16-core PC, and GPT didn't start it with multi threading in mind   ).

And I called it Asset Viewer, Scene Browser. Because without real content, it's just a scene with some animation playing when you click it. The day will come, but it's not today that an AI can make a fun MMO in a few prompts

comments.author: IAmTiiX
comments.body:
>Who needs to cut scope when AI can code things as fast as you can think of them?

That's the thing though. AI can't think of them. AI can't come up with ideas or be creative like you can. That's your strength as a human using AI as a tool. You come up with the ideas, have AI construct them, then you can go in with your knowledge and review what the AI is doing and suggest changes, and iterate.

Posts like these make it seem like AI is just doing all of the work on its own, but the AI wouldn't even be doing anything if it wasn't told what to do.

Use it as a tool and become someone who can use AI effectively to level up your development, instead of worrying that AI will just outright replace you.

replies.author: MuffDivers2_
replies.body:
I have almost no experience doing this stuff. I went to school for coding a few years back through a bootcamp. I gave up at some point. Now AI does it all for me and I am able to do things I always wanted to do in a weekend. Right now I have claude sonnet recreating brand new textures for Call of Duty (2003) and it's expansion. I just tell it what I want to do and it does everything it needs to do to get what I want done. It decrypted all the files and talks with my other programs. It ran a bunch of tests for me so I could pick the best look for new textures. I am using the original textures as a reference. Someone AI upscaled the COD textures a few years back. The mod never worked and it looked like crap compared to this. What I am doing right now looks great and it is not just an upscale. These are new beautiful textures. If one texture comes out bad, I review it and come back to it. A few days back I did the same for a old gamecube game called P.N.03. I tried to do it myself a few months back and it was okay. Claude made everything I had done so much better and I just had to guide it on what I needed done. I feel for op

AI cant come up with ideas?    Try it mate.  Feed it a few of your own then ask it to do 50 more.   Half will be great and several will be better than yours.

replies.author: IAmTiiX
replies.body:
Trust me, I've done lots of experimentation with AI as an idea generator, and most of the time it just comes up with very generic or boring responses. Even when I've given it some of my original ideas and asked it to come up with more, the results are pretty bad.

That being said, what AI has been really useful for, for me, is using it as a sounding board. I give it my ideas, then tell it to ask me questions that allow me to flesh them out. The AI isn't creating anything, it's just asking me questions that get me thinking about things that I maybe hadn't considered before.

replies.author: readytojumpstart
replies.body:
Trust me, ive literally sold hundreds of thousands in upsells at my company with many ai generated ideas.

Give it good start, it will indeed be additive.  Even sources feasible vendors in price range.  This was opus 5.  Sol 6.1 is even better and haven’t even tried 5.5 claude stuff

replies.author: IAmTiiX
replies.body:
Obviously I don't know what you do, but I just haven't found it to be very useful when it comes to creative ideas, like coming up with original game mechanics, or writing stories, or even coming up with story beats.

I do however think that you don't *have to* have an "original", or even particularly creative idea, for that idea to be successful. Fifa and Call of Duty are some of the most popular franchises ever, and they are also very copy-pastey and generic, year after year.

That's not to say that whatever you're using AI for is generic or copy-pastey. My point is just that something can be very successful even if that's the case.

Sol 6.1 is what I use, and it's been great as a coding assistant, but again, it just hasn't yielded good results when I use it as an idea generator for game development. Maybe my prompts are just bad, but I get good results with coding, so I'd like to think that I'm doing something right.
